planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plugs in spring into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants to knit together into a continuous mat by the following season.

directions: This cultivar forms a dense, woody-based mat of tiny aromatic leaves covered in midsummer by an unusually intense flush of crimson to deep purplish-red flowers, among the most saturated flower colors of the creeping thymes. It thrives in lean, fast-draining soil and resents heavy, wet, or richly fertilized ground, where it is prone to crown rot. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to tidy the mat and encourage dense regrowth for the following year. Use it between stepping stones, draping over low walls, or as a flowering groundcover in a hot, dry rock garden.

common_name: Russetings Creeping Thyme (Bronze-Green Rose-Pink Mat Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; the wiry trailing stems knit together quickly to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat.

directions: Russetings carries dark green foliage that can take on a subtle bronzed cast, topped in summer by a long-lasting, abundant display of deep rose-pink to purplish flowers that pollinators favor heavily. It is vigorous and wiry-stemmed, spreading steadily into a tight evergreen mat that tolerates drought, poor soil, and light foot traffic once established. Avoid soggy or heavy clay sites, where creeping thymes are prone to rot over winter. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage repeat flushes of color.

common_name: Pygmy Creeping Thyme (Dwarf Miniature Mat Thyme)

planting.note: Install small divisions or plugs in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing closely since individual plants stay extremely low and slow to fill in.

directions: One of the smallest-statured creeping thymes in cultivation, this dwarf selection hugs the ground even more tightly than typical mat-forming types, building a dense, moss-like carpet of tiny fragrant leaves. Purple-pink flowers appear in dense whorls in early summer and draw butterflies and other pollinators. It needs sharply drained, average to dry soil and full sun, and tolerates drought, shallow rocky ground, and urban conditions once established. Its extremely low, fine-textured habit suits tight crevices between paving stones, trough gardens, and rock garden plantings where larger thymes would overwhelm the space.
